claims.text: The investigated coating is a microwave-cladded Fe20Co20Ni20Mn20Cu20 high-entropy alloy on SS-304 steel.
The as-produced HEA coating has no preformed oxide layer.
A protective, mechanically robust oxide film is the key factor governing the coupled tribo-corrosion response.
The protective oxide film simultaneously reduces mechanical wear and corrosion kinetics.
Thermal annealing at approximately 800 °C induces a continuous protective oxide film on the HEA surface.
The protective film may consist of chromium oxide and high-entropy spinel phases.
The oxide layer acts as a physical barrier to chloride-ion penetration.
Chloride ions can penetrate or breach the coating and initiate localized corrosion.
The oxide layer acts as a physical barrier to mechanical abrasion.
Suppressing abrasion and chloride penetration reduces localized substrate removal and limits corrosion-site initiation and propagation.
Annealed samples will have lower total tribo-corrosion degradation than unannealed samples.
Annealed samples will have lower wear rates than unannealed samples.
Annealed samples will exhibit slower corrosion and improved passive-film stability relative to unannealed samples.
The unannealed baseline lacks the robust protective oxide film attributed to annealing.
Protection should persist while the oxide film remains adherent and intact.
Excessive mechanical stress or aggressive disruption of the oxide film should diminish its protective benefit.
The effect can be tested by comparing annealed and unannealed coatings under otherwise identical mechanical and electrochemical conditions in 3.5 wt% NaCl.
Failure to obtain statistically significant reductions in both wear and corrosion, or failure to detect a distinct protective oxide correlated with improvement, would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The film is alternately described as forming in situ during tribo-corrosion and as already present because it was created by a pre-test thermal anneal.
